title: What a Constitution Is
hook: The rulebook above the rules: a constitution sets out how a government is structured and the limits on its power.
key_points: A constitution is the highest-level set of rules defining how a state is organized and governed.
It typically establishes the branches of government, their powers, and how leaders are chosen.
It often guarantees certain rights and is harder to change than ordinary laws.
Constitutions can be written in one document, or uncodified across many sources.
content_html: A constitution is the foundational set of rules for a state — the framework that sits above ordinary laws and that those laws must respect. It generally lays out how the government is structured: what branches exist, what powers each one has, how leaders are selected, and how the parts relate to one another. Many constitutions also guarantee a set of basic rights that the government must protect.
extra_html: Because a constitution is meant to be the stable backbone of a political system, it is usually harder to change than a regular law — often requiring special majorities or extra steps. Constitutions come in two broad styles: codified, written down in a single authoritative document (as in the United States or Germany), and uncodified, where the rules are scattered across statutes, court decisions, and long-standing conventions (the United Kingdom is the classic example). Encyclopaedia Britannica surveys both. Either way, the constitution is the reference point against which the legitimacy of laws and government actions is judged.

related.title: How a Bill Becomes a Law
related.hook: An idea becomes binding law only after a journey: drafting, committee review, debate, votes, and final approval.

related.title: Separation of Powers
related.hook: Split government into branches that make, enforce, and interpret the law — so no single part can do all three.

related.title: Amending a Constitution
related.hook: A constitution has to last — but not freeze. Amendment rules let it change deliberately, usually demanding more agreement than an ordinary law.

related.title: Statute Law vs Common Law
related.hook: Not all law is written by legislators. Some of it is built up, case by case, by judges — and these two sources of law work very differently.

flashcards.prompt: What is a constitution, and how does it relate to ordinary laws?
flashcards.back_html: The highest-level rules for how a state is organized and governed — it sits above ordinary laws and is usually harder to change.

flashcards.prompt: Which of these does a constitution typically do?

choices.text: Establish the branches of government and how leaders are chosen
List the price of every public service
Replace the need for any other laws

flashcards.explanation_html: Constitutions set the structure of government, the powers of its parts, and often basic rights — ordinary laws fill in the details.

flashcards.prompt: Are all constitutions written in a single document?

choices.text: No — some are uncodified, spread across many sources
Yes, every country has one single written constitution
No country writes its constitution down at all

flashcards.explanation_html: Many countries have one codified document, but some (like the UK) have an uncodified constitution drawn from statutes, cases, and conventions.
